damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. PADDOCK - HAGRID'S HUT) - Malfoy's taunting before Buckbeak incident
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book establishes Malfoy as cunning and calculating: he is 'not fool enough to pick a fight right under a teacher's nose' (Scene 7), he plans and plots deliberately (Scene 52: 'Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle weren't listening; they were talking in an undertone and Harry had a nasty feeling they were plotting how best to disrupt the lesson'). His insult to Buckbeak ('Are you, you great ugly brute?') comes after he has been disdainfully patting the hippogriff, projecting false confidence and arrogance born of entitled superiority (Scene 62).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Malfoy pushes past Harry and strides toward Buckbeak impulsively, saying 'Give me a go at that thing. If Potter can do it, it must be easy.' The insult is delivered immediately and impetuously, without any of the book's deliberate plotting undertone. The film removes the beat where Malfoy has been observing with narrowed, malicious eyes and bowing successfully before insulting Buckbeak (book Scene 61 is absent from the film — there is no moment of Malfoy successfully patting the hippogriff before insulting it).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Malfoy insults Buckbeak from a position of false confidence after successfully bowing and patting him — his arrogance is calculating and self-assured. The film collapses this into impulsive recklessness, making him seem merely hot-headed rather than dangerously entitled. The loss of the successful bow-and-pat beat also removes the irony that Malfoy knew the rules and chose to break them anyway, which is central to his characterization as someone who flouts norms from a sense of superiority rather than ignorance.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. PADDOCK) - Malfoy's 'dementor behind you' taunt and Slytherin mockery
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book places Malfoy's dementor taunt outside the castle after the train arrival (Scene 13-16), as a public cruelty directed at Harry's vulnerability, with Malfoy 'elbowing past Hermione to block Harry's way,' his 'face gleeful and his pale eyes glinting maliciously.' It is a deliberate, targeted act of social humiliation. The Weasley twins separately confirm Malfoy 'came running into our compartment' during the dementor encounter on the train and 'nearly wet himself' (Scenes 27-28), establishing his own fear as the hypocritical backdrop to his mockery.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film transplants the 'there's a Dementor behind you' taunt into Hagrid's Care of Magical Creatures class (Film Scene 3), where Harry has just called Malfoy a 'stupid prat.' Malfoy delivers it as a quick deflection/counter when threatened, and the entire class joins in with an eerie mocking 'OOH' sound before laughing. The context strips away the targeted, premeditated cruelty and recasts it as a reactive classroom jibe with crowd participation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's dementor mockery is a studied, deliberate campaign of cruelty exploiting Harry's genuine trauma — amplified by the dramatic irony that Malfoy himself was frightened by the dementors. Moving the taunt to a reactive classroom moment, embedded in group laughter, flattens Malfoy's calculated malice into generic schoolyard teasing and loses the hypocrisy that makes the book moment so cutting.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (INT. GREAT HALL - NIGHT) - Malfoy performing injury for Slytherin audience
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book details Malfoy's performance of his injury extensively: he 'swaggered into the dungeon, his right arm covered in bandages and bound up in a sling, acting... as though he were the heroic survivor of some dreadful battle' (Scene 86). He winks at Crabbe and Goyle when Pansy looks away (Scene 88), explicitly showing self-aware manipulation. He uses the injury as leverage to have Harry and Ron do his potions work (Scenes 92-113) and openly admits to Harry it is 'partly' about getting Hagrid fired but also has 'other benefits' (Scene 113). The book gives extensive space to this scheming.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Malfoy briefly holding court at the Slytherin table (Film Scene 4), saying 'It comes and goes. Still... I consider myself lucky. According to Madam Pomfrey, another minute or two... and I could've lost the arm.' Ron calls him 'the little git' who's 'laying it on thick.' The scene is brief and observed from a distance by the Gryffindor trio. The entire Potions class sequence — where Malfoy weaponizes his injury to humiliate Harry and Ron and explicitly reveals his scheme to get Hagrid fired — is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Potions sequence is the payoff of Malfoy's scheming: it shows him actively wielding social power, manipulating Snape, humiliating Harry and Ron in detail, and revealing his calculated motives. Its absence removes a defining demonstration of Malfoy's cunning agency — his ability to turn victimhood into a weapon. The film reduces this to a brief observed performance, stripping Malfoy of his active role as antagonist-schemer and converting him into a passive object of contempt rather than a genuine threat.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (INT. LUPIN'S CLASSROOM) - Malfoy's Boggart class behavior
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not place Malfoy in the Boggart lesson as a participant with notable individual characterization beyond the general Slytherin/Gryffindor dynamic. The book's Malfoy is characterized throughout PoA by his deliberate, vocal cruelty and scheming — not passive muttering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film Boggart lesson (Film Scene 5), Malfoy's only contribution is a soft mutter: 'It's this class that's ridiculous.' He does not participate in the exercise, does not react openly, and is noted only as one of the Slytherins who doesn't laugh at Neville's Boggart result. Later in the same scene (Film Scene 6), Malfoy passes a parchment note to Harry via a moth — a caricature of Harry being struck by lightning — which Snape intercepts and reads aloud, embarrassing Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The moth-parchment gag inverts Malfoy's usual dynamic: rather than Malfoy being the one who lands a public blow, the scene results in Harry's embarrassment via Snape's intervention, which is more Snape's doing than Malfoy's. The soft mutter replaces the book's pattern of Malfoy making loud, contemptuous public comments. Minor damage to voice — Malfoy becomes a background snickerer rather than an active tormentor — but the corpus evidence for a strong book baseline here is limited, so impact is low.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (EXT. SHRIEKING SHACK) - Snowball ambush replaces mud/invisibility cloak confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Hogsmeade confrontation (Scenes 193-216) is a richly layered sequence. Under the Invisibility Cloak, Harry pelts mud at Malfoy's head while Malfoy taunts Ron about the Weasley family's poverty and mocks Hagrid's impending loss. Harry acts deliberately and with agency; Malfoy is humiliated in a way he cannot explain. The cloak is accidentally revealed, Malfoy sees Harry's disembodied head, screams and flees, and Harry must race back — creating genuine tension and consequences (Snape's interrogation). Malfoy's taunts about Hagrid ('I really wish I could hear that great hairy moron trying to defend himself') show his cruelty about Buckbeak's fate.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Film Scene 7) substitutes snowballs for mud, removes the invisibility-cloak-reveal tension, and adds Pike as a fourth member of Malfoy's group. Malfoy begins with classist taunts about the Weasleys' home ('Seems a bit grand for you, Weasel-Bee. Don't your family all sleep in one room?') and begins a racial slur toward Hermione ('filthy, little mud--') before being cut off by a snowball. The sequence ends with Malfoy being kicked in the rear and stumbling away, then Hermione and Ron also being knocked over by Harry. The scene plays as physical comedy. There is no Snape interrogation aftermath, no tension about the cloak being revealed, and no connection to the Hagrid/Buckbeak plot thread.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book sequence gives Harry meaningful covert agency — he chooses to act, successfully humiliates Malfoy, but faces real consequences when the cloak slips and Snape interrogates him. Malfoy's taunts specifically target the Buckbeak case, connecting his cruelty to the plot. The film converts this into broad physical comedy that ends with Malfoy simply being chased off. Harry's agency is present but the stakes, consequences, and plot connection are lost. Malfoy's partial slur ('mud--') is more overtly villainous than the book's classist insults in this scene, but his defeat is cartoonish rather than satisfying.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 (EXT. - near monoliths) - Malfoy spying on Hagrid before execution
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes (Scene 232-237) that Malfoy, Crabbe, and Goyle were 'standing just inside the castle doors, listening' as Hagrid broke down on the castle steps, then Malfoy says 'Look at him blubber! Have you ever seen anything quite as pathetic? And he's supposed to be our teacher!' This provokes Hermione's slap. The scene is about Malfoy's public cruelty toward a grieving adult.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Film Scene 10) shows Malfoy lurking with binoculars near stone monoliths, spying on Hagrid in the pumpkin patch feeding Buckbeak, and saying 'Did you see the big, fat blubbering oaf?! Oh, this is going to be rich. Did I tell you, Father said I can keep the head --' This is observed by Harry, Ron, and Hermione from a distance before Hermione's wand-and-punch confrontation. The 'Father said I can keep the head' line is a film addition.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Malfoy performs his cruelty publicly and directly, saying it to Hagrid's back in front of students at the castle doors — a brazen act. The film's Malfoy is spying covertly with binoculars, which makes him seem more furtive and less boldly contemptuous. The 'Father said I can keep the head' line adds a grotesque trophy-hunter quality not present in the book corpus. The shift from public contempt to private surveillance slightly mutes the social brazenness that defines book-Malfoy's cruelty, though both versions are cruel. The 'keep the head' addition also risks making Malfoy seem more cartoonishly villainous than calculatingly arrogant.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 (EXT. SUNDIAL GARDEN) - Hermione punches rather than slaps Malfoy
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Scene 238-243) describes Hermione slapping 'Malfoy across the face with all the strength she could muster. Malfoy staggered.' She then raises her hand again and draws her wand. Malfoy steps backward, and mutters 'C'mon' to Crabbe and Goyle, retreating into the dungeons passageway. Malfoy is visibly intimidated and retreats without making a threat.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film (Film Scene 11) shows Hermione jabbing her wand under Malfoy's nose first (he is 'cross-eyed with fear'), then after Ron says 'He's not worth it,' she lands 'a looping right to Malfoy's jaw, putting him flat on his back.' Malfoy 'leaps to his feet and runs.' The film then adds (Film Scene 13, time-reversal) that Malfoy, now under the bridge, says 'Not a word of this to anyone, understood! I'll get that jumped-up Mudblood one of these days. Mark my words...' and Hermione trips him a second time.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film amplifies Malfoy's humiliation (knocked flat, then tripped a second time) while adding his under-the-bridge threat ('I'll get that jumped-up Mudblood one of these days'), which slightly restores menace but makes him seem more reactive and impotent than the book's version, who retreats with cold composure ('C'mon'). The book's Malfoy steps back with wary calculation — he is not routed, just disengaged. The film converts his retreat into a rout followed by a private, face-saving threat, which diminishes his composed arrogance and makes him seem more of a coward.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 14 (EXT. - Firebolt reveal) - Malfoy's response to the Firebolt
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Scenes 178-185) shows Malfoy arriving 'for a closer look' at the Firebolt, his 'eyes glittering maliciously,' taunting Harry about dementors and parachutes. Harry fires back ('Pity you can't attach an extra arm to yours, Malfoy'). The Gryffindor team laughs. 'Malfoy's pale eyes narrowed, and he stalked away' to consult the Slytherin team about whether it was really a Firebolt. The exchange is a sharp verbal duel that Harry wins, and Malfoy's reaction is cold, calculating anger.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film (Film Scene 14), Malfoy is present in the crowd when Harry reveals the Firebolt. Crabbe and Goyle start to lick their fingers (mimicking others testing the wind), and 'Malfoy SLAPS their hands down.' There is no verbal exchange between Harry and Malfoy, no taunting, no comeback from Harry. Malfoy's role is reduced to a silent, contemptuous gesture toward his own henchmen.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Firebolt scene is a key moment in the Harry-Malfoy rivalry — Harry gets a clean verbal victory and Malfoy's jealousy and cold fury are established. The film removes the entire exchange, replacing it with a throwaway moment of Malfoy policing Crabbe and Goyle. The rivalry's texture — Harry's wit against Malfoy's malice — is absent, and the audience loses a beat where Harry demonstrably gets the better of Malfoy through confidence rather than luck or power.

main_damage_causes: Collapse of Malfoy's calculated, scheming agency into impulsive or reactive behavior — the film repeatedly removes the deliberate, premeditated quality of his cruelty (Potions class manipulation, Hogsmeade cloak sequence) that distinguishes book-Malfoy as a genuine threat rather than a comedic bully

Loss of the Harry-Malfoy verbal rivalry dynamic — key exchanges where Harry matches or outmaneuvers Malfoy through wit are either removed or defused, weakening the personal antagonism that drives much of the book's tension

Reduction of Malfoy's active plot function — his role in weaponizing the Buckbeak injury against Hagrid (the Potions class scheme) and the consequential Hogsmeade confrontation are condensed or replaced with physical comedy, stripping him of narrative agency and reducing him to an observed antagonist rather than an active schemer
